lines.x: The moment I stepped into this office, a strange noise came through my headphones... Doctor, is your audio system connected to the wrong device? Ah—the anti-surveillance system is running? My apologies. I will switch off the equipment I'm carrying at once.

It seems the wind has picked up outside again. When I was small, living in Bresk, I always worried that a strong wind would blow in at night and put out the stove fire. For many years I would be woken in my dreams by the sound of the Far North's wind—whether it still happens? Of course not. I am not asleep right now. Hm? That wasn't what you meant?

Something I don't understand? No, the document is perfectly clear. I look confused? Ah, that's because my two horns aren't quite balanced in weight. Tilting my head a little makes it less tiring. Are you interested in the antenna I modified? I could show you the schematics—ah, no, it doesn't actually hurt.

I've noticed that you often fall into deep thought. I rather envy that. My own thinking is always too shallow, so I tend to realize things far too late. An example? For instance, it was only on the night I heard the news from the Far North that I understood: my admission to the Imperial Polytechnic University was nothing more than something the Grand Duchess needed for her record. How ironic.

The people in the cities believed they could keep the tragedy of the mining district outside their doors. They were wrong. The city is not theirs—not even the door itself belongs to them. I left Brezhenoy, then I left Deity Grypherburg, and still I can hear those footsteps behind me.

After coming here, I met Ms. Mantra, and I finally found that voice. She and Ms. Raidian are both remarkable people. You're teasing me—I didn't come for an autograph. Although, if she really would sign something, I do have a few microphones I've been keeping—

At first I only read out the daily maxim on the university's student union radio. One day I hadn't had time to prepare, so I read something I'd written myself. Word of it got out, unexpectedly, and a student came storming up to me demanding that I read what he had written as well. Yes—that was Laleya.

Begin recording. A great deal of paperwork remains today, and the scheduled long-range communication test will have to be postponed once again—hm? Were you calling me? I'm only recording my diary. If you don't mind, I'll continue. I hope tomorrow's recording will not be interrupted again. End.

After I was sealed inside the blockade zone, I kept trying to call for help from the outside, but all I could reach was silence. Every day, the anxiety of that 'voicelessness' made me physically sick. And it turned out there was someone right beside me who could hear me the whole time—Fedya, that fellow—er, no. What should I call him?
If you'd like, I can play some soothing music to help you sleep. It's fine—I won't hear it once I put my headphones on, so there's no need to worry.

Doctor, I remember you—that distinctive waveform that appeared so frequently in Rhodes Island's encrypted signals. Just call me Botany; I'm used to being called that. 'Bookworm'—I choose to take it as a form of praise.

The picture's a little hard to make out—huh, the static on the screen got worse when I moved closer! Equipment interference? One moment, I'll switch off everything I'm carrying. It will only take a dozen minutes or so.

A commendation for what I've done? Thank you. I once picked up a Rhodes Island commendation bulletin from a corner of the university attic. The person I was then could never have imagined that one day I would receive one myself.

Thank you for the recognition, though I don't feel I deserve such an honor. The same medal carries a different weight depending on whose chest it rests against. I still have a great deal to learn from Ms. Mantra and my other comrades.
Operational comms channel connected. Beginning the test now.
This is Botany. Beginning timecode verification.
All units, maintain radio silence. We're moving out.
Target has appeared.
Keeping listening watch.
Awaiting a response.
Coordinates synced.
Botany, ready.
Listen—the wind of the Far North is right behind you!
Look—the torch is in your own hand!
Think—why is it that we fight one another!
Cry out—so that everyone can hear!
Radio silence lifted. We may cheer now. Doctor, this is a victory worth celebrating. Botany out.
Well done, Doctor. Botany out.
Botany out.
Calling all units, calling all units. Listen closely to my voice. I will lead everyone out.
The faint hum of machinery at work... a reassuring atmosphere.
Oh—did you hear something too?
You mustn't touch that horn. It won't shock you—it's just that if you brush it, a very loud noise starts up inside my head—ah. You believed me.
Arknights.

I don't know why, but the New Year lights here feel warmer than the ones in Deity Grypherburg, and the wind is far gentler. Look over there—some of the Operators have already started dancing... Would you like to try as well? Yes, I've just picked up a piece of music. You might like it.
Doctor, how are you feeling today? The briefing is already on your desk. Would you like me to read it to you? Then—here is today's news—

Doctor, quick, put on my headphones. Do you hear that odd beeping? Could you write it down for me? Thank you! Oh—it looks like some kind of code. If I translate it one signal at a time—that's it! It says 'Happy birthday!' The cake, though, is still on its way.

On the night the voice from the Far North rang out across all of Ursus, I realized that listening alone was not enough. Only by making a sound, so that more people can hear, is change possible at all. Even if each time changes only a little, even if that little is very small—Rhodes Island will be with me, won't it?
